title: The Boy Who Broke the Bank
tagline: One unpaid salary, eight retellings, and a riot outside the Pipalnagar Bank — Bond on the ecology of rumour.

overview.intro: Ruskin Bond’s comedy of rumour follows a single piece of information — the sweeper-boy Nathu has not been paid — as it travels from mouth to mouth through a small town, gathering additions at every stage until it arrives as catastrophe. Published in the collection “Night Train at Deoli and Other Stories”, the story is narrated in the third person with the affectionate irony Bond brings to Indian small-town life. The bank is healthy, its owner is holidaying in Kashmir, and its funds are in order; by the end of the week a mob is throwing stones at its doors, and the boy who broke the bank is the boy who did nothing at all. This chapter follows the chain of retellings link by link, reads the comic technique, and asks what Bond is saying about how communities make their own disasters.

learn.title: Before you read: Bond and the small-town comedy

blocks.text: Bond’s small-town stories are written from long acquaintance with their kind: a market, a bank, a barber’s shop, a set of households whose principal activity is conversation. “The Boy who Broke the Bank” is one of his comic pieces, and its engine is a favourite Bond subject — the gullibility of respectable society and the way it treats its smallest members as material. Read the opening as a lesson in proportion: the story begins with a sweeper-boy’s unpaid wages, a matter of a few rupees, and Bond allows the reader to see at once that the town will make something enormous out of it. The third-person narrator’s tone is important too: never cruel to the townspeople, perpetually amused by them, and careful to give each link in the chain its own perfectly reasonable self-justification. That is Bond’s satirical stroke — nobody lies, everybody exaggerates a little, and the sum of their honesty is a catastrophe. The comedy depends, finally, on the reader knowing what the town does not: the bank is sound and the Seth is away on holiday, so every respectable panic is measured against a fact hidden in plain sight.

items: Bond’s milieu: the Indian small town of market, bank and endless conversation.
Nobody lies; each retelling is only a little larger than the last.
The narrator is amused rather than angry, which sharpens the satire.
The reader holds the fact the town lacks: the bank is sound.

learn.title: The chain: one fact, eight versions

blocks.text: Published summaries lay the chain out precisely, and it is worth following link by link. It begins with Nathu, the sweeper-boy of the Pipalnagar Bank, sweeping the steps on the twentieth of the month without his wages and grumbling about a promised raise of two rupees. Along comes Sitaram, the washerman’s son, carrying freshly ironed clothes, who asks what is wrong and then carries the story to his next customer, Mrs Srivastava, recommending Nathu as a sweeper and mentioning that the bank has not paid him. Mrs Srivastava converts a unpaid wage into a generalisation: if the sweeper is not being paid, the staff must not be paid either. Under the tamarind tree in the market she passes the enlarged version to Mrs Bhushan, who rushes to her husband with the news that the bank is about to go bankrupt. Mr Bhushan tells Kamal Kishore, the photographer, who has no money in the bank but remembers that his neighbour Deep Chand does; Deep Chand, mid-haircut, leaps from the barber’s chair and tries to telephone the Seth — who cannot be reached because he is holidaying in Kashmir. The inability to reach him is taken as proof, and by evening the town knows that the bank has collapsed and its owner has absconded. Then comes the riot: depositors mass at the doors, the bank cannot pay every claim at once, stones are thrown, and the next morning Nathu sweeps the mess outside his own bank while Sitaram tells him, with splendid illogic, that he is the boy who broke it.

learn.title: The characters: Nathu, Sitaram and the town

blocks.text: Nathu is the boy of the title and the least powerful person in every room: a sweeper with a grievance of two rupees, he grumbles because grumbling is all his position permits, and he watches, baffled, as his complaint becomes a legend he cannot disown. Sitaram, the washerman’s son, is rumour’s first carrier — well-meaning, idle with information, and perfectly innocent of what he starts. The two ladies, Mrs Srivastava and Mrs Bhushan, are Bond’s comic masterpieces: respectable, energetic and constitutionally incapable of leaving a story smaller than they found it. Among the men, Mr Bhushan and Kamal Kishore transmit with efficiency, while Deep Chand, the barber’s customer, supplies the story’s instrument — the telephone call that fails and is read as confirmation. Seth Govind Ram, absent in Kashmir, is the fact the town cannot consult. And the town itself is the story’s true character: a community so bored and so credulous that a minor inconvenience becomes proof of disaster, and so energetic that it organises a riot before breakfast. Bond gives each of them a perfect reason, which is precisely how the catastrophe is assembled.

learn.title: Technique: comedy, irony and narrative pace

blocks.text: The story’s comedy is engineered, and three devices carry it. Delayed knowledge: the reader is told in the first paragraphs that the Seth is holidaying in Kashmir and the bank is doing well, so every subsequent panic is measured against a fact the participants lack — the reader laughs at the gap and never at the individuals alone. Escalation by scenes: Bond gives each retelling its own setting — a doorstep, a hallway, a tamarind tree, a photographer’s shop, a barber’s chair — and the changing scene makes the growing story feel like travel rather than repetition. And understatement at the climax: the riot itself is narrated with the same even tone as the market gossip, so that stones thrown at a bank sound like the natural conclusion of a conversation. There is also Bond’s characteristic irony about the poor: the beggar Ganpat, whose crooked legs have argued poverty for years, is up and running towards the bank the moment his money seems threatened, and the sweeper-boy whose wages started it all is blamed for a collapse that exists only in the town’s imagination.

items: Delayed knowledge: the reader holds the truth the town lacks.
Escalation by scenes: each retelling gets a new setting and a larger claim.
Understated climax: the riot narrated in the tone of gossip.
Irony about the poor: Ganpat’s running legs; Nathu’s absurd blame.

learn.title: Themes: rumour, appearances and the weak

blocks.text: The danger of rumour is the surface theme and Bond treats it as a natural phenomenon: rumour grows because each reteller improves the story in the only currency available — plausibility dressed as concern — and because no participant can afford to be the one who did nothing. Appearances against reality runs beneath it: the bank looks doomed and is sound, the Seth looks absconded and is on holiday, the beggar looks helpless and is brisk, and the sweeper looks like the culprit and is the only person who told the truth. The exploitation of the weak is the third theme and the story’s sharpest edge: Nathu’s genuine grievance — two rupees and an unpaid wage — is dismissed when it is small and punished when it has become enormous, so that the poor supply both the information and the blame. A fourth thread, lightly drawn, is boredom as the rumour’s fuel: a town with nothing better to do manufactures a catastrophe for the sheer eventfulness of it. The comedy never darkens into tragedy — Bond keeps the ending wry — but the reader is left counting who paid for the fun.

learn.title: For the examination, and what to verify yourself

blocks.text: This story is examined on its chain, so learn the chain: name, occupation, what each person added, and who passed it to whom. Short answers ask what Mrs Srivastava said to Mrs Bhushan, what Mr Bhushan did next, why the telephone call mattered — precision here is all. Longer answers ask about rumour as a theme, and the winning structure is to trace one unit of information through three or four retellings, showing what each adds, before drawing the moral. Technique questions about humour should cite the arrangement rather than any sentence — the reader’s early knowledge, the scene-by-scene escalation, the calm narration of the riot. Title questions deserve preparation: explain what Nathu did, what he is accused of doing, and why the difference is the story’s joke and its injustice together. As with every prescribed text on this page, the account here follows published summaries and guides; verify the details you intend to reproduce against your own copy of the story.

questions.prompt: What is Nathu’s grievance at the start of the story?
options: His wages are unpaid on the twentieth, and his raise has been denied
He has been dismissed without notice
His broom has been taken away
questions.answer: His wages are unpaid on the twentieth, and his raise has been denied
questions.explanation: Nathu is grumbling because the bank has not paid him and the promised raise of two rupees has not been given — a small grievance that becomes a legend.
questions.commonMistake: He is not dismissed; the unpaid wage is the whole complaint.

questions.prompt: Who first carries Nathu’s grievance into the town?
questions.explanation: Sitaram asks Nathu what is wrong on his delivery round and then mentions the unpaid wage to Mrs Srivastava when recommending Nathu as a sweeper.
questions.commonMistake: The ladies enlarge the story, but Sitaram is the first carrier.

questions.prompt: Why does Deep Chand’s telephone call convince the town?
options: Seth Govind Ram cannot be reached, and absence is taken as proof of flight
The line is dead, which shows panic
The police answer with a warning
questions.answer: Seth Govind Ram cannot be reached, and absence is taken as proof of flight
questions.explanation: The Seth is holidaying in Kashmir, so the call fails; the town reads the inability to contact him as confirmation that he has absconded with the funds.
questions.commonMistake: Nobody confirms anything — the failure of the call is the “evidence”.

questions.prompt: What is ironic about the beggar Ganpat in the story?
options: His crooked legs do not stop him running to the bank for his money
He alone knows the truth and keeps silent
He refuses to withdraw his savings
questions.answer: His crooked legs do not stop him running to the bank for his money
questions.explanation: The beggar whose deformity has argued poverty for years is up and running when his money seems at risk — one of Bond’s touches about appearances.
questions.commonMistake: He does not know the truth; he simply reacts to the rumour like everyone else.

questions.prompt: The Pipalnagar Bank is owned by Seth Govind Ram, who is holidaying in ______.
questions.explanation: The Seth’s holiday in Kashmir is the fact the town cannot consult, and his unavailability becomes the rumour’s strongest false evidence.
questions.commonMistake: The place matters: it is why the telephone call fails.

questions.prompt: What does Mrs Srivastava tell Mrs Bhushan under the tamarind tree, and how had she got the information?
questions.answer: She tells Mrs Bhushan that the bank does not have money to pay even its employees — she has come to know it from the sweeper-boy himself. In fact she learned only that Nathu had not been paid and intended to leave, and her conversation converts one unpaid wage into a general statement about the bank’s condition.
questions.explanation: Both halves are required: the enlarged claim and the small fact it grew from, which is the mechanics of rumour.
questions.commonMistake: Do not say she invented the story; she honestly over-generalised.

questions.prompt: What happens outside the bank when the rumour reaches the townspeople?
questions.answer: Depositors mass at the doors to withdraw their money; the bank cannot pay out every claim at once, which is taken as further proof of collapse; the crowd begins shouting and throws stones; and by the next morning the steps Nathu sweeps are littered with the wreckage of the night’s panic — stones and a broken gate.
questions.explanation: The answer must include the sequence — queue, inability to pay, violence, morning aftermath — because the escalation is the story’s point.
questions.commonMistake: The bank never actually fails; the riot is the failure of the rumour, not of the bank.

questions.prompt: Trace the rumour from Nathu’s grievance to the riot, showing what each person adds.
questions.answer: It begins as truth: Nathu, unpaid on the twentieth and denied a raise of two rupees, tells Sitaram he will leave the bank. Sitaram, recommending Nathu as a sweeper to Mrs Srivastava, mentions that the bank has not paid him — still accurate. Mrs Srivastava performs the first enlargement: from one unpaid wage she infers that the bank cannot pay its employees at all, and under the market tamarind tree she tells Mrs Bhushan exactly that. Mrs Bhushan supplies the conclusion the sentence invites — if employees are unpaid, the bank must be about to go bankrupt — and hurries to her husband. Mr Bhushan tells Kamal Kishore, who has no money in the bank but remembers that his neighbour Deep Chand does; alarm now travels as advice. Deep Chand leaps from the barber’s chair and telephones the Seth, who cannot be reached because he is in Kashmir; the failed call is read as flight, and by evening the town holds the final version: the bank has collapsed and its owner has absconded. Depositors then mass at the doors, the bank cannot pay every claim instantly, stones are thrown, and the riot that follows is entirely the rumour’s child — the bank’s funds were never in question.
questions.explanation: Every link is named with its specific addition, and the answer closes by contrasting the town’s belief with the bank’s actual state.
questions.commonMistake: Do not skip links; the marks lie in the accumulation.

questions.prompt: How does Bond create humour in the story? Explain with reference to his technique.
questions.answer: Bond builds the humour on knowledge, structure and tone. Knowledge: the reader is told early that the Seth is holidaying and the bank is doing well, so every subsequent alarm is measured against a fact the participants lack, and the comedy lies in the widening gap between belief and the reader’s information. Structure: each retelling receives its own scene — a doorstep, a hallway, the tamarind tree, the photographer’s shop, the barber’s chair — and the change of setting gives the growing story the freshness of travel, so that repetition never feels repeated. Tone: the narrator keeps the same even, affectionate irony from the first sentence to the riot, so that stones thrown at a bank are narrated with the calm of market gossip, and the understatement lets the reader supply the outrage. Finally, Bond’s comedy is democratic but pointed: everyone is gently mocked, and the sharpest touches fall on the treatment of the weak — Nathu’s truth being worth nothing until it was large enough to be a crime, and Ganpat’s crooked legs forgetting themselves at the thought of lost money.
questions.explanation: Each device is named and located in the story’s events, and the answer ends on what the humour exposes, which is what a technique question requires.
questions.commonMistake: Do not merely say “the story is funny”; the devices and their locations carry the marks.

questions.prompt: The story suggests that nobody in Pipalnagar lies, yet a disaster is manufactured. Discuss how ordinary conversation produces the crisis, and who pays for it.
questions.answer: Every link in the chain is defensible in isolation, and that is Bond’s subject. Sitaram tells a friend’s trouble to a potential employer — common kindness. Mrs Srivastava, possessing one fact, uses the only inference available to her, since a sweeper unpaid is genuinely a bad sign. Mrs Bhushan, hearing of a bank about to fail, warns her husband to protect a neighbour, which is civic duty. Kamal Kishore points out the man whose money is at risk; Deep Chand acts at once, and his irritation at the failed call is human. The town, gathering the assembled version, withdraws its money like the depositors of any bank under threat — the run on the bank is precisely what the rumour would predict if it were true. Disaster is therefore manufactured out of accuracy failing gently at every step: no lie, only enlargement, and each enlargement sheltered by the reteller’s good name. Who pays? Nathu, whose true and tiny grievance is transmuted into the crime of breaking a bank, and who must sweep the stones the next morning; the bank’s staff, whose livelihoods are disrupted; and the town itself, which has proved how quickly it will believe the worst of an institution that held its money. The comedy is Bond’s, but the bill is collective — and the story leaves the reader understanding that rumour is not a failure of character but a property of conversation without verification.
questions.explanation: The answer walks each reteller’s justification, shows disaster as an emergent product rather than a lie, and answers the “who pays” question with the story’s own images.
questions.commonMistake: Do not hunt for a villain; the question exists to show that none is needed.
